name: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
title: Weighing the Scientific Consensus
answer: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across a body of research on a given question, rather than relying on a single study or a headline. It sits within literature review and evidence synthesis, where the goal is to map what is known, how strongly it is known, and where disagreements remain. On this site, the library holds 135 research papers and 12646 claims extracted from research works, which provide material for studying how consensus claims are made and supported.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Weighing the scientific consensus means assessing how much agreement exists across a body of research on a given question, rather than relying on a single study or a headline. It sits within literature review and evidence synthesis, where the goal is to map what is known, how strongly it is known, and where disagreements remain. On this site, the library holds 135 research papers and 12646 claims extracted from research works, which provide material for studying how consensus claims are made and supported.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on literature databases, reference managers, and systematic review platforms, along with AI tools that assist with screening, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. This site catalogues 732 AI tools and 800 scientific models, many of which support these tasks, though the core infrastructure remains the published record and its metadata. A glossary of 686 terms helps keep definitions consistent when different fields use the same words differently.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners start with a focused question, then search for studies, screen them against inclusion criteria, and extract data into structured tables. They assess each study for risk of bias and look for publication bias, then combine results through meta-analysis or narrative synthesis. Certainty is often graded using frameworks like GRADE, which separates the strength of evidence from the size of an effect. The aim is to show not just what the studies say but how much weight the overall body of evidence can bear.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Provenance matters because a claim about consensus is only as good as the studies behind it, so each statement should trace back to the original paper rather than to a secondary summary. This site follows that rule by linking to the original paper and never to the Consensus search tool, which keeps the chain of evidence visible. Risks include overstating agreement, ignoring contradictory findings, and failing to disclose funding or conflicts of interest. Reviewers also need to respect copyright when quoting or reusing figures, and to credit authors properly.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward living reviews that update as new evidence appears, rather than static documents that age quickly. AI tools are taking on more of the screening and extraction work, which shifts the reviewer's effort toward judgment and interpretation. There is growing interest in making the underlying data and code openly available so that consensus claims can be checked and rechecked. The harder problem is not finding more papers but weighing them well when methods, populations, and outcomes differ.
